verdict: Mode: design review of villanelle's language concepts (not the bindings). I read grammar/Villanelle.g4, grammar/villanelle.ebnf, docs/language.md, spec/spec.md, spec/glossary.md, spec/README.md, design/RECORD.md, .claude/errata.md and fixtures/rasl/*, and ran 25 probe configs through the real Python API (scratch: /Volumes/Dock/tmp/vil-review/lang/probe*.py). Verdict: FAIL. The syntax core is good: the grammar is proven free of ambiguity, the tree loses no text, a broken line never hides its neighbours, quoting means text, and a variable is always a whole value. Three concepts are not sound, though. First, a statement can end two ways (a line break or `;`), and a directive may be named with a number. Together these split a statement in two without any error: `ranges 0.0627\n 0.922;` reads as two directives, one named `0.922`. Second, variables have no single scoping model. Snippets look names up where they are written; included files look them up where they are included. An included file's top-level `set` lines leak into the block that includes it, so a reusable file that sets its own default cannot be included twice in one block (E5002). Overrides win over every `set` of a name at any depth, so `--set name=x` turns both of split/main.conf's per-place sinks into `x`, with no diagnostic. That breaks the owner's 2026-10-25 requirement that "each instance of the file would have its own bindings". Third, rules that depend only on the text are scattered. They sit in hand-written code in each binding (the check of a values text, which has already drifted once), in render-time checks (a bad escape or a non-integer bound is invisible to `parse` and to the graph), and in a user guide (docs/language.md is the only place the scoping and precedence rules are written down). A third binding's author cannot build from the spec. Smaller problems: two identical quote styles turn `'C:\temp\new'` into a tab and a newline without a word; `plain` brings back YAML-style type guessing; `use` is reserved in every block (nginx's `use epoll;` fails); and `:` is banned in words that start with a digit only so slices can parse, which turns `07:30` and MAC addresses into errors. What must change: pick one statement terminator; write one scoping and precedence model with a normative home in spec/ (included file as its own scope; overrides only for declared names); move every rule that depends only on the text into the grammar (a values-text entry rule, escapes, literal bounds) so no binding writes it by hand.
rootCauses: The rules about names (scope, visibility, precedence, statement boundaries) were grown feature by feature: snippets, include blocks, overrides and one-set-per-block each brought their own rule, checked by conformance cases. No single model was designed for them, and they have no normative home. docs/language.md, a user guide that calls the grammar 'the specification of the syntax', is the only place they are stated; spec.md has no section on scope or precedence. So five precedence regimes exist that nobody chose as a whole.

The grammar was checked for ambiguity, not for typos turning silent. Spelling choices made to serve one consumer's syntax (slice ':' banning colons in words that start with a digit, two statement terminators, two identical quote styles) put their cost on config authors as silent misreads rather than located diagnostics.

Rules that depend only on the text live outside the one source (the grammar). The check of a values text is a hand-written probe-and-scan in each binding. String escapes and literal slice bounds are value rules applied at render. So they are duplicated per binding (they have already drifted: errata 2026-10-29), and a tool working at the syntax layer or the low level never sees them.

findings.title: Two statement terminators plus directives named with a number split a statement in two with no error
findings.where: grammar/Villanelle.g4:9 (directive : header (separator | block)), :14 (separator : ';' | NEWLINE), :29 (WORD's NumberStart branch lets '0.922' be a directive name); docs/language.md:12
findings.evidence:
Probe 8: 'ranges 0.0627
    0.922;' renders as two directives, `ranges 0.0627` and `0.922` (no values), with diagnostics []. 'matrix 1 0 0
  0 1 0;' becomes `matrix 1 0 0` and a directive `0` with values `1 0`. Probe 4: 'color #ff0000;' renders `color` with no values and diagnostics []: the comment swallowed the ';' the author wrote, and the line break ended the statement anyway. 'a 1 # note ; b 2;' loses `b 2` silently. The same model causes E2008 (Allman braces refused: 'node a
{' gives E2008) and the whole line-break family of the check of a values text (spec.md:273-281).
findings.impact: Config authors coming from nginx (every rasl fixture ends lines with ';') who wrap a long `matrix` or `ranges` line get a wrong config and no diagnostic. rasl would read a node directive named '0.922'. This is a failure class, not one instance: any line break or comment inside a directive is a silent boundary.
findings.fix: Choose one terminator. nginx's model (';' required, a line break is plain whitespace) makes the split impossible. It also deletes E2008 and the line-break half of spec 2.8's check of a values text. Optionally keep directive names from starting with a digit or '-', so even a forgotten ';' gives a located error. HCL's model (line break only, no ';') is the other consistent choice. Owner question 1.

findings.title: An included file's top-level `set` lines join the including block, so a reusable file cannot set its own default and cannot be included twice
findings.where: docs/language.md:197-203 ('An included file's top-level set and snippet are seen after the include line in the including block, and count for that block's one-per-name checks'); spec.md:551-552; py/src/villanelle/include.py:1-3
findings.evidence: Probe 1: s.conf = 'set $port 80; node $name { port $port; }', included twice in one block with different `$name`. The result is E5002 at s.conf:1:5 'variable set twice in one block: $port', and the second copy's set line is unreadable. Probe 2: the includer sets $pixels 1 and s.conf sets $pixels 2: E5002, and inside the file `inner $pixels` reads 1, the includer's value. Probe 3: `include "s.conf" { set $host A; }` makes the file use A, but the includer's next line reads the file's default (`after default`). Probe 4: an included file reads the including block's local `$local` (dynamic scope), while a snippet body reads only variables visible where the snippet is written (lexical scope).
findings.impact: Breaks the owner's requirement (2026-10-25: 'each instance of the file would have its own bindings') as soon as the file declares anything. A file's own names collide with names in whoever includes it, so files cannot be composed. Authors face two scoping rules for two ways of reusing text.
findings.fix: One lexical scoping model for every way text is reused. An included file is its own scope, like a snippet body or a Terraform module. Its top-level `set` lines are defaults that the include line's block replaces, and nothing it declares leaks out. Anything it needs from outside is passed in its include block, as Apache mod_macro and Terraform modules require. If 'export definitions to the includer' is wanted (C #include style), make it an explicit, separate statement. Do not make it a side effect of where a `set` sits.

findings.title: Overrides are undeclared and global by name: they beat per-place include bindings and nested local variables
findings.where: docs/language.md:89-92; spec.md:625-628 ('An override wins over every set of its name')
findings.evidence: Probe 5: split-style main.conf with `include "s.conf" { set $name leds; }` and `{ set $name porch; }`, loaded with overrides {name: 'x'}. Both nodes render as `node x`, with no diagnostic. Probe 6: 'a { b { set $host inner; target $host; } }' with override host='"cli"' renders `target "cli"`. The precedence regimes now are: inner set shadows outer; an include-block set beats every set in the file; an override beats every set and every include-block set; a snippet parameter beats an override. All of them are only in prose, scattered over language.md:77-92, 146-148 and 197-200.
findings.impact: rasl's `--set host=...` can clobber any variable of that name in any included file at any depth. Duplicate node ids follow silently. An author cannot tell which names a program may replace, and a program cannot tell which names are meant to be replaced.
findings.fix: Bind overrides only to names declared to receive them: Terraform root-module `variable` blocks (module locals cannot be set from the CLI), or Nix `--arg`, which binds only the top function's formals. For example, only `set` lines at the root file's top level count, or an explicit declaration marks them. An override with no such name is then a misuse error at load, and a nested local or a per-place binding can never be reached. Write one precedence table in the spec. This is Make's command-line-variable semantics, a known footgun. Owner question 2.

findings.title: The language's rules about names (scope, visibility, precedence, splicing) have no normative home in spec/
findings.where: spec/spec.md:19-21 ('The language itself ... is in docs/language.md'); docs/language.md:3-5 (calls the grammar 'the specification of the syntax' and says the page 'adds the rules the load applies'); spec.md has no scope or precedence section (grep for scope/precedence/visible finds only E5001/E5003 rows and 5.1's one sentence)
findings.evidence: Five precedence regimes and three visibility rules (from a set's line on; a snippet sees sets written after it but before the use; included files see the includer's names) appear only as bullet lists of examples in a user guide. spec.md 5.1 restates one sentence of them. I had to probe to learn that an override beats an include-block set (probe 5), because no page says so.
findings.impact: A third-language binding author (the owner's 2026-10-28 ask: 'approach it like a specification' so new languages are easy) must reverse-engineer the semantics from the load conformance cases. Every finding above passed review because no single model exists to check a rule against.
findings.fix: Add a normative 'Expansion semantics' section to spec/, on the pattern of the CUE spec's 'Declarations and scopes' or the Nix manual's let/with/inherit rules: environments, how each statement extends one, the lookup order, and one precedence table. docs/language.md then teaches it and links to it, rather than being the source.

findings.title: The check of a values text is hand-written per binding as a probe-and-scan, instead of being a grammar rule
findings.where: ts/src/written/document.ts:817-859 (valuesTextProblems, moreThanValues, boundTextProblems); py/src/villanelle/written/_document.py:858-920 (values_text_problems, _line_break_problem, _bound_text_problems); spec.md:265-293; .claude/errata.md:177-191
findings.evidence: Both bindings parse `x <text>;` (or `x [<text>];`), re-parse with an inserted line break when the last token is a comment, then scan for SEMI, braces, COMMA and NEWLINE by hand. The errata record that they disagreed on three inputs ('1\n2 # c', '1 \\ # c', '[1, # c'), and TypeScript skipped the check for a blank text. Spec 2.8 carries about 18 named cases to defend this one splice.
findings.impact: Every new binding re-implements a subtle scanner that has already drifted once. The rule's real definition is 'what two bindings agree on', not the grammar, which goes against 'one source of truth per rule' and the codegen ask.
findings.fix: Add entry rules to Villanelle.g4 (for example `valuesText : SPACE* (value (gap value)*)? SPACE* EOF`, where a trailing COMMENT or a NEWLINE outside a list cannot be derived; `listItemText`; `boundText : (WORD | VARIABLE) EOF`). Every generated parser then gives the refusal and its position, and tools/check.sh proves it free of ambiguity like the rest. The hand scanners and most of spec 2.8's case list are deleted. With finding 1's ';'-required terminator, the line-break rule disappears entirely.

findings.title: `set`, `snippet` and `use` are reserved in every block, and extensions reserve names, in the directive namespace with no way out
findings.where: docs/language.md:212-216; spec.md:201-202, 535-536; spec/schema/api.json `reserved names`; py/src/villanelle/extension.py:24-40
findings.evidence: Probe 7: 'events { use epoll; }' (a real nginx directive) gives E5003 'unknown snippet: epoll'. A directive name must be a WORD (grammar :11), so `"use" epoll;` is no way out either. Whether `include "x";` is a directive or a splice depends on which extensions the processor was given: the same text means two things, and a formatter or editor working on the text alone cannot tell. The 'extension' port is include with a pluggable path function. `specs()` may only return file specs; the core owns splicing, include-block `set` semantics, E5012, and E3001/E3004 (named after include). So an extension cannot define any other meaning.
findings.impact: Domain vocabularies lose ordinary verbs (`use`, `set`) at every depth. The file's meaning leaks the program's processor setup (a policy leak into the text). The word 'extension' promises generality the port does not have.
findings.fix: Put meta-statements in their own space with a token no directive name can start with: UCL's `.include`/`.priority` macros, or KDL v2's '#'-prefixed keywords. For example, take one sigil out of NameStart and write `@set`, `@snippet`, `@use`, `@include`. Reserved names then cannot exist, and an unknown `@name` becomes a located 'no extension for @name' error instead of a silent directive. Name the port for what it is (an include source or splice rule) until a second kind of extension exists.

findings.title: Both quote styles process escapes, so there is no raw or multi-line string, and Windows paths silently corrupt
findings.where: grammar/Villanelle.g4:30-31 (STRING: the '"' and '\'' branches are identical); grammar/villanelle.ebnf:60 (EscapeText); docs/language.md:37
findings.evidence: Probe 3: "path 'C:\\temp\\new';" reads as ['C', ':', '\t', 'e', 'm', 'p', '\n', 'e', 'w']: a tab and a newline, with no diagnostic. 'C:\\Users' gives E4003, and only at render. No form holds a line break or a control character (spec.md:898-903), and \\u is still open (vil-m8w.2).
findings.impact: Authors writing paths, regexes or cron-like text get silent changes or late errors. Two quote styles that mean the same thing are a concept with no job.
findings.fix: TOML's split: single quotes are literal (no escapes, the raw string form), and double quotes keep the six escapes. One grammar edit, and the second quote style earns its place. If multi-line text is needed, add it as its own token (TOML ''' or KDL's raw strings), not as escapes.

findings.title: The `plain` reader brings back YAML-style type guessing on top of a sound untyped-word model
findings.where: spec/spec.md:344 and 371-374 (plain's one rule); docs/language.md:48-51
findings.evidence: Probe 2, `plain()` results: `version 1.10` gives 1.1 (the '10' is lost); `zip 01234` gives '01234' (text) but `zip2 12345` gives 12345 (a number); `big 1e400` gives '1e400' (text) because it overflows; `neg -0` gives 0; `flag2 yes` gives 'yes'. The value's type depends on its spelling and size, not on what the program asked for.
findings.impact: Programs that take `plain` as the convenient reader inherit YAML's 'Norway problem' class. This is exactly what the explicit readers (`number`, `integer`, `boolean`, `word`) and 'quoting means text' were built to rule out.
findings.fix: Keep the nginx model: a word has no type, and the program's reader decides. Make `plain` lossless and stable, for example a tagged result whose text is always kept (word, string, list, slice, index), or drop it and let the high level (vil-xlo) map a declared schema to the typed readers. A word's type should never depend on its magnitude.

findings.title: Slice and index are not orthogonal to the rest of the language, and their ':' costs every author
findings.where: grammar/Villanelle.g4:17 (slicedWord : WORD '[' bounds ']': the base is only a WORD), :29 (no ':' in words that start with a digit or '-'); docs/language.md:36, 85; design/RECORD.md:23
findings.evidence: Probe 11: 'snippet s $src { connect $src[0:3]; }' gives E2009, so a snippet cannot slice its parameter, although a variable may be a bound (`a[0:$n]`). Probe 9: 'at 07:30;' and 'mac 00:1a:2b:3c:4d:5e;' give E2001 at the ':'. `color:hsl` works only because it starts with a letter. The ':' ban exists so a bound `1:2` does not lex as one WORD.
findings.impact: rasl's channel-range syntax shapes the general lexicon. Times, MAC addresses and IPv6 must be quoted, and the reuse feature (snippets) cannot be combined with the slice feature.
findings.fix: Treat a subscript as a postfix on any atom a name can stand for (WORD or VARIABLE), so every value form combines with every other. Pick a slice separator outside the word alphabet, so ':' can return to every word. The owner picked the ':' rule (RECORD.md:23, a revisable pick), so offer him that trade with its cost.

findings.title: Errors that depend only on the text (bad escape, a literal non-integer bound) are invisible to `parse` and to the graph
findings.where: grammar/villanelle.ebnf:52-55 ('value rules ... applied after parsing'); spec.md:450 ('diagnostics MUST be empty exactly when the input is in the grammar's language'), :654 (graph diagnostics MUST NOT include E4xxx)
findings.evidence: Probe 2: for 'p "a\\qb";\nc x[foo:bar];', parse diagnostics are [], graph.diagnostics are [], and render diagnostics are [E4003, E4001].
findings.impact: A formatter, editor or language server built on the syntax layer or the low level reports a broken file as clean. An edit that writes `"\\q"` passes the edit check and only fails a later render.
findings.fix: A rule that depends on one token's text belongs to the syntax layer. Restrict STRING's escape alternative in the grammar (`'\\' ["'\\ntr]`, with the bad form as its own error token, as UNTERMINATED_STRING already is), and report a literal non-integer bound from `parse`. Only a bound reached through a variable stays a render-time E4001.

findings.title: 'One set per name per block' does not deliver one meaning per block
findings.where: docs/language.md:75-78; spec.md:165; design/RECORD.md:71
findings.evidence: Probe 4: 'set $x 1;\nn { v $x; set $x 2; w $x; }' renders `v 1` and `w 2` inside one block, with no diagnostic. `set` is visible only from its line onward (not hoisted), so a name already changes meaning partway through a block. Meanwhile probe 13 ('set $a 1; x $a; set $a 2; y $a;') is E5002, and yet `y` still renders with 1. Probes 1-2 show the rule is what turns an include into a collision.
findings.impact: The rule refuses honest reassignment and still allows a name to change meaning partway through a block. It reads as a patch, not an invariant.
findings.fix: Choose one of two consistent models. Single assignment per scope with hoisting (Terraform locals, Nix `let`): every reference in a scope sees that scope's one binding, wherever the `set` is written. Or sequential rebinding (nginx `set`, OCaml `let` shadowing): reassignment is allowed and the line order decides. Either rule can be stated in one sentence and enforced the same way for snippets and includes.

findings.title: 'set' names five things across language and API (vil-r8s)
findings.where: spec/spec.md:727-739 (stated cost); glossary.md:72; spec.md:838 (variable kind `set`)
findings.evidence: The keyword `set`, statement kind `set`, variable kind `set`, the edit `set (text)` and `set override (name, text)` are all spelled 'set'. The variable kinds mix a keyword (`set`) with concept words (`parameter`, `override`).
findings.impact: Docs must keep saying 'not the language's set line'. A program reads `v.kind === "set"` next to `v.set(...)` and `graph.setOverride(...)`.
findings.fix: Keep the keyword (nginx's `set $var value` is the right prior art) and the owner's `set (text)`. Name the variable kinds by concept, the way `parameter` and `override` already are, for example `assigned` or `local`. The kind word then never repeats a keyword or a method name.

good: The grammar is held to two proofs: Bison with %expect 0 shows the syntax has no ambiguity, and g4overlap shows no two token kinds can match the same text. Planted bad grammars prove the checks fail. A predicate, action or lexer mode is refused, so none can hide a conflict. This is stronger soundness than nginx, UCL or HCL have.

The tree loses nothing: every character sits in exactly one token, for broken input too. Comments belong to statements by LibCST and Roslyn style trivia rules, and edits keep layout. That is the right base for round-trip editing, on a par with tomlkit and ruamel.yaml.

Errors never stop the read: a bad line becomes one unreadable statement in its place, later siblings are kept, and a diff can say 'unknown' rather than 'removed'. This is the Roslyn and tree-sitter posture, and correct for editors.

Untyped words with typed readers (the nginx model) are sound. Quoting means text ('"8080"' is never a number). Number words are exactly JSON numbers, and a located E4002 or E4004 points at the user's text when the program asks for the wrong kind.
'A variable is always a whole value' rules out shell- and Make-style string interpolation bugs: `fps$x` is E2009, never joined.

Snippet and use follow Apache mod_macro (`<Macro>`/`Use`): snippets have their own namespace (`use universe` never looks at a directive), the arity is exact, and a body exports nothing. Snippet bodies use lexical scope, which is the right model; the trouble is that includes do not follow it.
A file included in many places is read once and its syntax errors reported once (the owner's note honoured). Cycles, expansion depth and directive count have named limits with their own codes.

The diagnostic registry is sound: codes are stable, banded by phase, retired codes are never reused, there are no warnings, and program codes live in their own `namespace/name` space that cannot collide.
questions: How should a statement end? Recommended: (A) ';' is required and a line break is plain whitespace (nginx), with directive names unable to start with a digit. Cost: authors must type ';' (every rasl fixture already does), and a file's last directive with no ';' becomes an error. In return: the silent statement split cannot happen, E2008 goes away (braces may sit on their own line), long directives may wrap, and the line-break half of the check of a values text is deleted. Alternative (B): line break only, and ';' is no longer a terminator (HCL). Cost: every rasl file and fixture must be rewritten, and lists stay the only way to wrap a line.

Which variables may a program override, and what does an included file see? Recommended: (A) one lexical model. An included file is its own scope: its top-level `set` lines are defaults its include block may replace, and nothing leaks out to the includer. An override binds only names `set` at the root file's top level, and an override of any other name is a misuse error at load (as with Terraform root variables or Nix --arg). Cost: split/sink.conf must receive `$pixels` through its include blocks (`set $pixels $pixels;`) instead of reading it from main.conf, and a program cannot reach a nested variable without the author lifting it to the root. Alternative (B): keep today's model and write it down. Cost: per-place bindings remain one `--set` away from being overwritten, and reusable files still cannot set their own defaults.

verdict:
Mode: design review of the domain model across layers, run against the canonical spec. The repo has no .claude/gates.json. I reviewed against spec/ (glossary, spec, contract, codegen, api.json, diagnostics.json), AGENTS.md and the owner-design vocabulary, and I wrote and ran probes against both bindings (scripts in /Volumes/Dock/tmp/vil-review/). Verdict: FAIL.

The parts are well built: precise handle and detach rules, a single check for text-only edits, variants that carry their kind, a layer direction enforced by lint and tests, and a shared conformance driver. The domain cut between the low level and the rendered layer is in the wrong place, though. The low level's `expand ()` already builds the whole rendered tree. `render` is a 40-line reshaper (ts/src/rendered/render.ts) that copies it into a second set of node types. One value is spread over three per-kind families (written, expanded, argument), 22 value-related types in all. The upstream cause is that the extension port sits in an "io" layer below the low level, even though the spec says it must be pure. That forces a handle-free "expanded value" family into "shared", which forces a third family on top.

api.json is not yet a specification that could drive bindings. It is a hand-kept list of names. Its types are free text, about ten type names in it are never defined anywhere, 21 per-language differences are written as prose, and the error lists are incomplete. The generator reads about 5% of it (kind lists, codes, limits). The per-language type names it stores can be derived for 72 of its 73 concepts.

The error groups contradict their own rule. DetachedError is listed as a program bug but sits under VillanelleError. The same bad name raises two different error groups depending on the method called. In TypeScript, misuse and wrong-type errors are the same class. The glossary's "one word, one meaning" rule is broken by its own rows: `override`, `place`, `written` and `definition` each mean several things.

What must change:
1. Decide one owner for expansion. The rendered tree should build on the expansion's nodes instead of copying them, and the extension port belongs in the low level.
2. Make api.json a typed interface description: a real type grammar, every referenced type defined, spellings derived from the casing rule, and the error lists checked against spec 2.8. Generate the per-kind type skeletons from it.
3. Rebuild the error class tree on the spec's own two sorts, "program bug" and "expected outcome".
4. Give each overloaded word one meaning, with a check in the generator.
5. Generate every fixed fact a binding or doc repeats by hand, and delete the hand copies. That covers the unreadable reason passed at each call site, the hard-coded set of render-only codes, and the code tables in the docs.
rootCauses: Layer membership was chosen to satisfy import rules, not the domain. The extension port is filed under "io" although spec 5 requires it to be pure (api.json:34; spec.md:521). Its use must hold handle-free values, so a third value family ("expanded value") went into "shared". Then expansion, which load itself needs, had to live in the low level, which leaves the rendered layer as a copy of the low level's expansion with a few extras (parents, walk, closest, addresses, diff). Most of the duplicate-tree, duplicate-name and diagnostics findings follow from this cut.

The schema is a list of names, not a typed interface description. Types are prose strings, per-language differences are prose `spell` notes, and per-binding spellings are stored instead of derived. A generator cannot build type skeletons or error contracts from it, so every binding keeps hand-written copies of facts the schema already holds (the unreadable reason for each code, which codes are render-only, type names), and the prose docs drift from the spec.

The glossary is a table nobody checks mechanically. "One word, one meaning" is stated (glossary.md:24) but no check enforces it, so rows that overload a word (override, place, written, definition) and fields whose name is a concept word but hold text (`override.variable`, `extension.directive`) got into the canonical pages.

findings.title: Two trees with the same shape and three per-kind value families: the rendered layer re-copies the low level's expansion
findings.where: spec/spec.md:908-951 (6.10, including its own 'Cost' paragraph at 949), spec/spec.md:962-979 (7.0); ts/src/rendered/render.ts:22-46; py/src/villanelle/rendered/_tree.py; spec/schema/api.json concepts 'directive expansion', 'value expansion', 'expanded *', '* argument'
findings.evidence: render.ts is about 40 lines that map each directive expansion to a directive, each value expansion to an argument and each unreadable expansion to an unreadable. Python probe (probe1.py) output: DirectiveExpansion ['block','origin','statement','unreadable','values'] against Directive ['block','closest','error','name','origin','parent','unreadable','values','walk','written']; ValueExpansion ['chain','definition','items','value','written'] against WordArgument, whose class chain is _Links then ExpandedWord, with the same links flattened in. Counting value types: 6 written + 5 expanded + 5 argument + 3 unions + slice value, index value and plain value = 22. Five of the argument variants add no members of their own in api.json (word, string, slice and index argument have 0; list argument re-types items). The same handle has two names: `directive expansion.statement` and `unreadable expansion.statement` against rendered `directive.written` and `unreadable.written`, while `value expansion` uses `written`. This is a glossary breach inside a single layer.
findings.impact: Binding authors write and keep in step about 25 near-duplicate types for each language, and a third binding triples that. Integrators must learn which value type they hold in each context (an extension sees an expanded value, a config reader sees an argument, an editor sees a written value plus a value expansion), and they meet the same link under two names. Every new value kind or link changes three families in every binding.
findings.fix: Pick one owner for the expanded tree and compose from it; do not copy it. Load needs expansion (include paths can come from $vars), so the low level owns it. The rendered `directive` and `argument` should then build on the expansion's nodes, the way `word argument` already extends `expanded word`, adding only parent, walk, closest, address and error. Collapse the expanded and argument families into one per-kind family that is parameterized by its links. Prior art: 'Trees that Grow' (one tree shape parameterized by phase); LibCST and Roslyn, which attach derived facts (metadata providers, SemanticModel) to one tree rather than building a second one; Lightbend Config (HOCON), which solves the same problem (includes, substitutions, origins, text-only edits through ConfigDocument) with two layers and no third tree. good: The layer direction is enforced mechanically, not by convention: an ESLint import ban plus a Python ast scan (api.json 'layer check'). render builds only on public members; a duck-typed object with only expand() and root rendered correctly in the Python probe.

Operations exist only on the variants where they can succeed (no NoSetLineError; `set` is absent from parameters and override variables). This is a compile-time guarantee in TS and an AttributeError in Python, the strongest guarantee available in each.

The text-only edit rule has one check with one message pointing to quote(), and load and set override share one override check (spec 6.3). The probe showed the same ValueError from both for a bad name.
The handle and detach contract (spec 6.1 table) is a real contract: which handles each edit keeps, what each edit returns, and the ordering (detached before the type check, before everything else).

contract.md decides positions per string unit with one conversion point in the shared driver (conformance/driver/units.py), and gives the line-break rule and the number edges. Those are the hard cross-language edges, written down once.

The shared conformance driver with small per-binding adapters (ts 199 lines, py 297) replaces two hand-written runners, and the expected outputs are derived by hand, not recorded from an implementation.
Kind lists, codes and limits are generated at build time and not committed. The generator tests itself with planted broken copies (gen-api.py planted()), so the check is known to catch errors.

The alternative, keeping it in 'io' with plain-data values, keeps the three families.

Should TypeScript kind lists become generated runtime enumerations (`StatementKind.Set`), reversing spec 2.10's 'no TypeScript constant objects', to match your 2026-10-29 ask for 'proper enumerations instead of hardcoded strings'? verdict: Mode: a language expert's review of the Python binding py/ (the concept review already ran, so this does not repeat it). The repo has no .claude/gates.json, so I reviewed against spec/ (binding-guide.md, spec.md, contract.md, schema/api.json), py/README.md and the owner-design vocabulary. I read every public module and the private modules the findings rest on. I ran mypy --strict and ruff on the package (both clean) and seven user programs in /Volumes/Dock/tmp/vil-review/py/. Verdict: FAIL. The typed surface is unusually good for a young library. Every variant has `kind: Literal[...]` and `__match_args__`. mypy narrows on both `kind` and `isinstance`, and it refuses an operation on a variant that lacks it. Edits refuse non-text with a clear TypeError, and the exceptions mix in builtins the way `json.JSONDecodeError` does. rasl's task (load, read the leds host, change `$leds_host`, save, diff) ran correctly on the first try. Where it fails is the places a Python developer gets hurt without the type checker noticing. First, a port typed `Sequence[str]` accepts a bare str and quietly splits it into one-character file specs. Second, the natural edit loop over a render raises DetachedError on the second copy, and the README asks users to remember a workaround. Third, `str(BadTextError)` is just "bad text: E2001", and its diagnostics leak the binding's internal probe text. Fourth, a lost update cannot be told apart from a disk error except by reading the message. Fifth, the spec's own rule that two values are the same when their texts match is not what `==` does. Below these sit a shape problem and a duplication problem. The shape problem: the binding is a hand-made port of TypeScript's structure and of api.json's prose. Return types (list here, tuple there), container shapes, names that shadow builtins and the error tree are all chosen by hand, method by method, and only checked afterwards by a test that parses prose with regexes. The duplication problem: keyword dispatch and precedence tiers are hand-typed strings in two places. What must change: generate the class skeletons, return types, `__all__` and the error tree from a typed api.json; type the ports so a str cannot pass; give a lost update its own error type and give `BadTextError` a readable message; make value equality follow spec 2.9; settle what happens to a value handle after an edit (see the questions).
rootCauses: The binding is a hand port, not a projection of the spec. api.json gives types and Python spellings as prose (`text[]`, `"spell": {"py": "diff(after, /, *, key=None)"}`), so every class skeleton, return type, container shape and exception class is chosen by hand. tests/test_api_names.py then parses those prose spellings with regexes, and checks only one direction. That is why `read`/`save`/`diff` return lists while every other `x[]` is a tuple. It is also why the rendered block and the written block have different shapes, five Argument classes repeat the same `__init__`, and the internal layout mirrors TypeScript's free functions over shell classes (40 function-local imports in model.py, about 155 reads of other classes' private attributes).

Rules that depend only on the text live in binding code, not in the grammar (concept lens 1's root cause 3, seen from Python). The check of a values text parses a made-up `x <text>;` line, so its diagnostics show text the user never wrote. The keywords `set`, `snippet` and `use` are compared as raw strings in two separate dispatchers. The scoping tiers (`"parameter" | "set" | "forced"`) are a private Literal that matches no public kind list.

The Python model was declared to be the `ast` style everywhere (binding-guide.md:88), with identity and live handles, and nobody weighed the value-object side the owner pointed to ("Python should take inspiration from pydantic", 2026-10-24). So plain data has identity equality, refusals carry no type or readable message (a bare code, a lost update as RuntimeError or OSError), and an edit made through a snapshot detaches the handle that every other copy shares.

Should an edit that replaces one value with one value keep its handle, the way `Statement.set` and `rename` already do? verdict: Mode: binding review (TypeScript, ts/) as a library a TS developer would adopt. The repo has no .claude/gates.json, so I reviewed against spec/ (binding-guide, codegen, spec 2.8, 6.9, 7.0), ts/README.md, docs/*.md and the owner-design vocabulary. I wrote, typechecked and ran 10 user programs against the built package: strict, noUncheckedIndexedAccess, exactOptionalPropertyTypes, verbatimModuleSyntax and skipLibCheck false (scratch: /Volumes/Dock/tmp/vil-review/ts-user/). Verdict: FAIL. The everyday type model is good. Kinds are checked string-literal unions, narrowing needs no cast, a switch over a kind is proven exhaustive, codes are an `as const` object, and the rasl task (load, read the leds host, change $pixels, change one include copy's host, save) compiles and runs with no cast in user code. But the types stop at exactly the places where an integrator gets hurt. (1) Villanelle text and a program string are both `string`, so `server.set(userInput)` silently writes two values. (2) A render over a graph with an unread include drops directives with no diagnostic, and `diff` reports them as `removed`, which is wrong for rasl's hot reload. (3) The extension port cannot be used from the public API: the first-party include extension reaches into package internals. (4) A lost update on save is a plain `Error` that can only be told apart by its message, and each writer words that message differently. (5) Rules the spec says "a program could have checked" are not exported for checking. On top of that come the structural costs for binding authors. The adopted naming rule says TypeScript writes `DocumentGraph`, but the package puts 114 names, 76 of them with an `I` prefix, in one flat namespace. The interfaces are typed by hand, and a 450-line run-time probe checks names that the compiler would check if they were generated. And the low level casts through `unknown` 15 times. What must change: give villanelle text its own type; make an unread copy visible in the render; build `include` on the public extension port; add a typed lost-update error; export the generated rules; export per-layer subpaths with names that differ from the spec only in casing; and generate the TS interfaces and error classes from a typed schema, so `tsc` becomes the public-name check.
rootCauses: The binding types what the spec names as data, but not what the spec names only in prose. 'Villanelle text' versus 'a plain string' (spec 6.9), 'lost update' (spec 4.x writer rows), 'unread copy' (spec 7.0) and 'a name the program could have checked' (spec 2.8 misuse) are each a distinct state in the spec, yet in TS each is a bare `string`, a plain `Error`, an absence, or a hidden regex. So the compiler cannot see the failures integrators actually hit, and each one is guarded by a sentence in the README (a convention). Several of these trace to concept-level gaps: the spec has no error group for a lost update, no render result for an unread copy, and no schema type for villanelle text.

The public surface is written by hand per binding instead of generated from the schema. So the TS interfaces, error classes and spellings are typed out by hand (68 stored `"ts": "I…"` spellings in api.json against adopted rule 1's casing-only rule), names are checked at run time by a 450-line probe, and the internals cannot connect the concrete classes to the public unions without `as unknown as`. This is the TS face of concept lens 2's finding that api.json is a list of names, not a typed interface description.

One flat namespace for three layers. Every layer re-exports through `villanelle`, so names must carry their layer by ad-hoc marks (`IWord` is written, `IDirective` is rendered, `IExpandedWord`, `IWordArgument`, `ISliceValue`). Containers and walks differ per layer, and internal-only types (`ValueRef`) leak. Python already splits `villanelle.written`; TS does not.

verdict: Mode: design review (DRY and code generation) of the villanelle checkout at /Volumes/Dock/Home/Code/villanelle/.claude/worktrees/binding-spec. The repo has no .claude/gates.json, so I reviewed against spec/ (codegen.md, conformance.md, schema/api.json, schema/diagnostics.json), AGENTS.md and the owner-design vocabulary. I read tools/gen-api.py, both adapters, the driver and the binding modules they mirror, and ran probes for mypy and tsc (scratch: /Volumes/Dock/tmp/vil-review/dry/). Verdict: FAIL. The base is sound: generated output is never committed and is rebuilt on every build, token kinds come from the grammar, `--check` proves itself with planted broken copies, and there is one shared driver. But generation stops at names. It produces 449 lines (codes, kinds, limits). Against that, each binding has about 6,000 hand-written source lines (TS 5,974, Py 6,217), and 15 files call themselves a port of the other binding. The public shape is declared three times (api.json's 73 concepts, 93 hand-written TypeScript interfaces, the Python classes), and only a 669-line test that inspects objects at run time ties those copies together. The casing rule is written 7 times and the copies already disagree. The diagnostic code table exists in three copies: spec.md and diagnostics.json disagree on 8 of 32 meanings and 14 of 32 "found by" entries. Python's StrEnum lets a misspelled bare string through mypy --strict (probe), where TypeScript refuses it (TS2367). The adapter protocol and its 20 data shapes are prose, written by hand in each adapter, and some field names use TypeScript's spelling. The target I propose: api.json grows into a typed interface model shaped like the Language Server Protocol's metaModel.json (plain JSON, a JSON Schema that checks it, a typed type grammar, typed per-language overrides). From it, each binding gets generated interface declarations, data records, error classes, typed diagnostic constructors, the kind-to-class lookup tables, a module of names in the binding's spelling, the docs tables and the conformance data shapes. The algorithms, the parser runtime glue, sync or async I/O, iteration and option styles stay hand-written, held in step by the shared cases mapped to spec rules. Several binding duplications are really concept problems that generation must not freeze: the statement keywords, the variable precedence rule, the render-only codes and the value text rules. Those need the concept fixes first. What must change: make api.json a typed model and generate the interfaces (compile-time conformance) and diagnostic descriptors from it; give the casing rule, the adapter protocol and the docs tables one generated home each; replace every free-text field a tool parses with typed data.
rootCauses: The schema stops at names. api.json has no type grammar (87 distinct free-text type strings, 7 that name nothing), no typed per-language overrides ('spell' is prose that three tools parse with regexes), and no data-shape definitions. So it cannot generate interfaces, constructors or conformance shapes. Each binding re-declares the shape by hand, and a test that inspects objects at run time keeps them in step: a test-time guarantee where a compile-time one is available.

Facts that belong to a code, kind or concept are re-stated where they are used instead of looked up from one generated descriptor. That covers a code's unreadable reason (19 call sites per binding), its detail text, whether render owns it, a kind's variant class, an error class's group name, and a member's parameters (the driver's OPS table). Three prose copies (spec.md 2.4, docs/rendered-tree.md, diagnostics.json) are kept by hand and already disagree.

The algorithms are kept in step by porting TypeScript line by line, not by building each binding from the spec. Rules that depend only on the text live outside the grammar (concept lens 1: keywords, value text rules, escapes), and there is no single scoping model (lens 1). So each binding hand-writes them, and they drift (errata 2026-10-29).

findings.title: `spell` is one free-text field that mixes four different things, and three tools parse it with regular expressions
findings.where: spec/schema/api.json (21 `spell` entries); tools/gen-api.py:75-78 (`spelled`); ts/src/api-names.test.ts:84-93 (`keyOf`); py/tests/test_api_names.py:41-45 (`leading`)
findings.evidence: Of the 21 entries: 10 map a member to a language protocol (people form to `toString()`/`str()`, count to `length`/`len()`, iterate, collect to a `with` block, statements to 'the block itself is a Sequence'). 5 are call-signature notes ('load(path, *, overrides=None)', 'walk(*, descend=None), a generator'), 1 is a type ('ReadonlyMap<string, string>'), and 5 are a note that `set` shadows a builtin. keyOf needs a special regex rule ('A type spelling ... keeps the name's casing'), and `spelled` extracts 'RESERVED' from 'RESERVED (written/bind.ts)'.
findings.impact: The language-specific spellings, which are where each binding gets its idiom, are the part a generator cannot read. A fourth kind of note would break three parsers in different ways.
findings.fix: Replace the field with typed traits, closed lists the schema checks: `protocol: display | length | iterate | sequence | context`, `options: keyword-only | options-object`, `result: generator | callback`, and per-language `name` overrides only where the rule cannot apply. Each emitter maps a trait to its idiom once (`display` becomes `__str__` or `toString()`). Prior art: Smithy traits; the Pulumi package schema's typed `language: { nodejs, python, go }` override blocks.

findings.title: gen-api.py and api.json are not yet the shape of a real interface definition; the repo's reasons for rejecting existing tools are partly wrong, though JSON is still the right size
findings.where: tools/gen-api.py (536 lines, one file); spec/codegen.md:126,140 ('api.schema.json proposed, not written'); spec/schema/api.json:3329-3428 ('removed in milestone 1/2', 24 entries), 'disagreements' (11 prose entries)
findings.evidence: The generator builds each language's output by joining strings inside one script, and validates the JSON's shape by hand (check_concepts and the Model constructor, roughly 120 lines) because no JSON Schema exists. The schema mixes the model with history ('removed in milestone 1/2') and prose notes on where the bindings differ. Per concept lens 2, the 87 type strings are free text (7 name nothing: 'definition', 'diagnostic code', 'key rule', 'locatable', 'plain value', 'result', 'token range'). codegen.md:126 rejects TypeSpec as 'aimed at HTTP services', but TypeSpec's core language (models, enums, unions, interfaces with operations, decorators) is protocol-neutral: HTTP is one library, @typespec/http, and custom emitters are supported. Smithy's core model is also protocol-neutral.
findings.impact: Adding a language means adding more functions to the same file. Adding a type feature means changing hand-written validation. A generator cannot emit signatures from prose types.
findings.fix: Target: keep JSON (the owner, 2026-10-25: 'JSON scheme is a nice foundation, where it works'), shaped like the LSP metaModel. Add a JSON Schema that checks the model. Type references become a small closed grammar (`{kind: base|reference|array|map|or|literal|optional}`). Concepts carry nature, layer, members, errors and traits. Diagnostics carry typed templates. Kind lists, grammar-derived lists, limits and value text rules live alongside. Move history to git and the binding differences to the binding guide. Split the generator into a loader/validator plus one emitter module per target (about 300-500 lines each). Generated per language: kinds, codes and descriptors, names, interfaces/Protocols, records, the error class tree, lookup tables, constants, docs tables, data-shape selections. Hand-written: algorithms, the ANTLR runtime glue and recovery strategy, I/O ports and sync or async style, protocol idioms, module layout, docs and examples (the owner, 2026-10-26: generated shapes 'not conducive to building natural APIs that are idiomatic in each target language' unless idiom is expressed per language). Revisit TypeSpec with custom emitters only if the hand-made type grammar starts to grow features like generics, mixins or templating. Cost: retyping 231 members once, plus one emitter per language.

findings.title: The value text rules live in a second, unchecked grammar file and are translated into regexes and tables by hand in each binding
findings.where: grammar/villanelle.ebnf:1-7 (header '@rasl/config language, grammar draft 2 (round 11)'), :55-63; ts/src/values.ts:6-59; py/src/villanelle/_values.py:12-74; tools/check.sh (checks only Villanelle.g4)
findings.evidence: NumberText, IntegerText, BooleanText and EscapeText (the 6 escapes) are defined in villanelle.ebnf. Each binding re-types them: the INTEGER_TEXT and NUMBER_TEXT regexes, `ESCAPES`, the canonical escape table and `true`/`false` (values.ts:36-59; _values.py:50-74). check.sh never compares the EBNF with the .g4, and the EBNF's last commit is the round-11 grammar change. api.json's 'patterns' block already generates one regex (VARIABLE_NAME) for both bindings, with the Python `\Z` handling done correctly once.
findings.impact: A third binding hand-translates the EBNF a third time, and an edit to the value rules can miss one binding. The two grammar files can drift with no check.
findings.fix: Concept fix first (concept lens 1, root cause 3): move rules that depend only on the text into the grammar so the generated parser enforces them. Whatever remains goes into the schema's patterns and tables (number, integer, boolean words, escape decode and encode tables) and is generated as VARIABLE_NAME already is. Retire the EBNF or derive it from the .g4. Cost: small, the generator path already exists.

findings.title: Facts that come from the grammar are hand-mapped in each binding: the rule-to-node-kind table and the statement keywords
findings.where: ts/src/syntax/walk.ts:32-39 and py/src/villanelle/syntax/_walk.py:16-23 (rule name to node kind: `lastDirective`, `slicedWord`); ts/src/written/shape.ts:~45-75 and py/src/villanelle/written/_shape.py:52-71 (`name.text == "set" / "snippet" / "use"`); generated RESERVED (api.json 'reserved names')
findings.evidence: Both bindings carry the same 6-entry table from grammar rule names to node kinds, while villanelle.ebnf already marks the same rules (`/* cst: directive */`). The keywords `set`, `snippet` and `use` appear as bare strings in each binding's shape check, a second home next to the generated RESERVED set that holds the same three words. Python's shape check also compares `shape.kind == "set"` against a StrEnum (finding 3).
findings.impact: Renaming a grammar rule breaks two hand tables (caught at import, which is good). Adding a keyword means editing the schema and two shape switches.
findings.fix: Derive node kinds from the grammar, as token kinds already are: label the concept rules (for example an ANTLR `// cst: directive` comment convention read by gen-api, or rule-name suffixes) and generate the table. That follows tree-sitter's node-types.json, which is generated from its grammar. Generate a keyword list with one home that both the shape check and RESERVED use. Concept tie: concept lens 1 finds that keywords outside the grammar are why `use` is reserved in every block and why E5009-E5011 are text rules applied by each binding. Making them grammar tokens or rules would delete both shape modules (119 + 112 lines).

findings.title: The error class trees are written twice by hand, and the adapters recover the error group from class names by regex
findings.where: ts/src/errors.ts (93 lines, 6 hand-typed `this.name = "..."`); py/src/villanelle/errors.py (79 lines); ts/conformance/adapter.ts:182; py/conformance/adapter.py:274; conformance/driver/written.py:27; spec/schema/api.json 'error groups'
findings.evidence: api.json holds each group's name, parent and fields, but each language's built-in base class is prose ('subclass of VillanelleError and ValueError'). Both adapters turn `constructor.name` back into words with `(?<!^)(?=[A-Z])`. In TypeScript, a minifier renames `constructor.name`, and the package has a browser entry (ts/src/browser.ts). The driver's ERRORS table maps group names to TypeScript class names.
findings.impact: Programs and adapters have no stable value to tell error groups apart other than class identity or class name. A third binding writes the tree by hand again.
findings.fix: Generate the class tree from 'error groups': parent, built-in base per language as a typed field, fields, and a readonly `group` (the spec name) plus `sort` ('program bug' or 'expected outcome') on every class. Adapters then read `error.group`. Prior art: AWS SDK v3 exceptions carry `name` and `$fault`, generated from Smithy's `@error("client"|"server")` trait. Concept tie: concept lens 2 found that the tree contradicts its own sorts (DetachedError, misuse error being TypeError in TS). Fix the groups first, or generation will copy the contradiction into every language.

findings.title: The algorithms are kept in step by line-for-line porting from TypeScript, not built from the spec, and they have already drifted
findings.where: 15 files say they are ports (py/src/villanelle/written/_bind.py:7, _document.py:3, _shape.py:4, _values.py:2, rendered/_render.py:5; ts/src/syntax/recovery.ts:9 'the Python port copies them line for line'); py/src/villanelle/written/_bind.py:271,389-399 and ts/src/written/bind.ts:225,317-349 (the private 'parameter'|'set'|'forced' precedence); .claude/errata.md:177-191
findings.evidence: Python modules name their TypeScript source, two of them by stale paths (ts/src/ast/anatomy.ts does not exist). The variable-precedence rule `_pick` and its private three-word kind list ('forced' is a third word for an override or include-block `set`) are written in each binding. Errata of 2026-10-29: 'The two bindings took different readings' of the order of the values-text comment check. TypeScript skipped the override check for a text that trims to empty. Python's old runner had a latent unit bug.
findings.impact: TypeScript is the de facto reference, against the owner's 2026-10-27 'Within villanelle I want the spec to win over a reference language'. A third binding would port TypeScript, not the spec, and would inherit its slips.
findings.fix: Codegen is not the answer here. Instead, number the spec's rules and map every shared case to the rule it pins, so a rule with no case is visible. Prior art: test262 tags each test with the spec section it covers (`esid`). Express pure decision tables such as classifyError as ordered data in the schema, run by a 10-line loop in each binding. Concept tie: `_pick` is the scoping model concept lens 1 says nobody designed. Write that model once in spec/ before pinning it, never generate the current five precedence rules.

findings.title: Several closed sets are not lists at all: reader names, the adapter's hello units and levels, operation names, 'found by'
findings.where: spec/conformance.md 4.1 (readers 'word', 'string', 'number', 'integer', 'boolean', 'list', 'slice', 'plain'; units 'utf-16'|'code point'|'byte'; levels 0-4); conformance/driver/units.py:12; ts/conformance/adapter.ts:155; py/conformance/adapter.py:253; diagnostics.json 'found by' (free text such as 'readers (expanded value, argument)')
findings.evidence: The reader names are members of 'expanded value' in api.json and a prose list in conformance.md, with no list the schema checks. Four of them reuse value kind words ('list', 'slice', 'string', 'word'), so one word has two meanings, and in Python `list` and `slice` hide the builtins (value.py:49). The unit and level words are typed out in units.py, both hello replies and the docs.
findings.impact: Small today. These are the next places a binding or the driver spells a word differently.
findings.fix: Make each one a kind list in the schema, generated like the others, including a module the driver can import (it needs a plain-constants form, because the driver targets Python 3.9 and StrEnum arrived in 3.11). Concept tie: the reader and kind word collision is a glossary question for the owner ('one word, one meaning', glossary.md:24).

good: Generated output is never committed and every build, test and typecheck regenerates it (tools/gen.sh calls gen-api.py after ANTLR), so no stale copy can exist and no freshness check is needed. This follows the owner's 2026-10-23 rule.
Token kinds come from the grammar's lexer rules (gen-api.py grammar_tokens), their one home. The hand-written TokenKind in both bindings was deleted.

`gen-api.py --check` runs planted broken copies of the schema (deferred member, missing variant, wrong kind, bad parent) and fails if one is not caught, so the checks are known to work (tools/check.sh step 4).

TypeScript kind lists are string-literal unions, not `enum`. That is the right idiom: Node 24's type stripping, which the adapter relies on, rejects `enum`, and the probe shows tsc refuses a misspelled kind (TS2367).

Python variants type `kind` as `Literal[StatementKind.SET]` on StrEnum lists, which narrows under `match` in a pydantic-like way. The generated VARIABLE_NAME regex handles Python's `$`-before-newline trap once (`\Z`), for every user.
Messages fill `{limit}` placeholders from the limits block, so a limit's number has one home in every message (gen-api.py ts_message/py_message).
diagnostics.json's stored ts/py spellings are checked against the casing rule, so that redundancy cannot drift silently. It is still redundant (finding 5).

There is one shared driver, with positions converted and bytes compared in one place (test262/eshost prior art, named in conformance.md 1). It is the right place to build the selection-based adapter of finding 4.
questions: Should the schema become the source of every public signature, with generated TypeScript interfaces and Python Protocols that hand-written classes must implement, moving the line codegen.md:115 drew at 'only fixed lists and data records'? Recommended: yes, with idiom expressed through typed per-language traits (protocol, options style, generator or callback), so each binding still reads natively. Cost: api.json needs a type grammar and every one of its 231 members is retyped once. About 300-500 lines of emitter per language. Wait until concept lens 2's value-family and tree decisions are made, so generation does not freeze types that should be deleted. In exchange, 93 hand-written TypeScript interfaces and most of the 669 lines of name tests go away, and name drift becomes a compile error.

Should each conformance adapter become a generic walker that resolves members by spec name, driven by selections the driver derives from api.json, instead of 20 hand-written data shapes per binding? Recommended: yes. It makes the protocol's data shapes and the public-name check one mechanism, and removes TypeScript spellings (savedText, replaceWithText) from the neutral format. Cost: the driver must read the schema, a run makes more or larger requests (about 1 s per binding today), and an adapter can no longer shape a data shape by hand where a binding's object model differs.
